title: Why Braking Later Can Make You Slower

pronunciation.telemetry: technical values are illustrative on-screen graphics

segments.text: Braking later looks faster. But does it make you faster?
segments.delivery: Open with a short pause after faster; let the question land before the corner entry.
segments.visual_cue: Two cars approach the corner under the headline BRAKE LATER. LOSE TIME?

segments.text: The red car brakes late and carries more speed into the corner. The cyan car brakes earlier and turns in sooner.
segments.delivery: Use a clean contrast between the two strategies; avoid rushing the second sentence.
segments.visual_cue: LATE BRAKE and EARLY ROTATION trajectories, braking markers, TURN-IN and APEX callouts appear.

segments.text: The late-braking car enters faster, but it runs wider and waits longer before applying throttle. The earlier car rotates cleanly and gets back on power sooner.
segments.delivery: Build the sentence through enters faster, then soften briefly before the consequence: waits longer.
segments.visual_cue: RED / ENTRY and CYAN / EXIT telemetry panels compare entry speed, throttle delay, and throttle timing.

segments.text: And that difference compounds all the way down the straight. The car with the better exit starts pulling away.
segments.delivery: Increase momentum through the first sentence; give pulling away a decisive finish.
segments.visual_cue: Both cars exit onto the straight; the cyan car gains a visible gap beneath EXIT SPEED WINS.

segments.text: So the fastest entry is not always the fastest lap. Protect the exit, and the lap comes to you.
segments.delivery: Slow slightly for the first sentence. Deliver the final clause as the takeaway, with a brief pause before it.
segments.visual_cue: The racing-line comparison freezes under ENTRY SPEED ≠ FASTEST LAP.

mix.notes: Keep engine and transition effects audible at beat boundaries, but duck them under explanatory sentences. Do not add narration over the final 0.25 seconds so the takeaway can resolve cleanly.
